slots.sample: Long trips are won or lost in the planning spreadsheet, but the spreadsheet does not need to be complicated.

Work out a daily target for food, beds and local transport, then double it for the first week while you calibrate — every destination has a real cost of living, and you will not know yours until you have spent it. After that, track spending weekly rather than daily; daily tracking becomes a chore nobody keeps up.

Book the big-ticket, hard-to-change items — flights, visas, a trekking permit — before you leave, and leave everything else loose. Overplanning a three-month trip wastes the exact flexibility that makes it worth taking three months in the first place.

Build in one splurge a month and one true rest week with no sightseeing at all; both keep budget trips from curdling into endurance tests. The cheapest way to see more of a place is usually to slow down, not speed up — fewer moves, fewer transport costs, fewer wasted travel days.

slots.sample: Ninety-six miles from the outskirts of Glasgow to the foot of Ben Nevis, Scotland's oldest long-distance path earns its reputation one boggy mile at a time.

I started at Milngavie, the unglamorous suburban trailhead marked by a granite obelisk, and within two days the path had already traded pavement for the open moor of Rannoch. The route runs north along Loch Lomond's eastern shore, a section locals warn you about more than any other, since it narrows to a scramble over tree roots and boulders for several hours near Inversnaid.

Camping wild is legal and common here, and I pitched most nights within sight of water: Loch Lomond, Loch Tulla, the River Orchy. The middle days across Rannoch Moor are the emotional heart of the walk, a flat expanse of heather and old drove roads with Buachaille Etive Mòr rising like a broken tooth on the horizon.

Book the Kingshouse or Inveroran for at least one night if you'd rather have a bed and a dram than a tent — both sit right on the route and fill up fast in summer. The path ends in Fort William beneath Ben Nevis, and if your legs have anything left, the extra day up Britain's highest mountain is worth tacking on before the bus home.
Inés Carvalho

slots.sample: Called the finest walk in the world since a Victorian-era journalist coined the phrase, Milford Track still lives up to it across four days through Fiordland.

Access is tightly controlled — a boat in across Lake Te Anau, a single direction of travel, a fixed number of hikers per day, and three Great Walk huts booked months in advance for the November-to-April season. I crossed Mackinnon Pass on the second morning in a rare clear window, the kind locals say happens on maybe one day in three given Fiordland's rainfall.

The descent off the pass runs beside Sutherland Falls, one of the tallest waterfalls in the country, close enough that the trail gets a fine mist on breezy days. Sandflies are the real hazard here, not weather — I wore repellent from the first hour and still spent an entire evening in a hut common room being quietly eaten alive.

Book through the Department of Conservation the moment the season opens; huts sell out within hours for the popular months. If independent hiking dates don't work, guided trips run the same route with private lodges and hot showers, at several times the price but considerably less logistics.

slots.sample: Tokyo's food day runs backwards: it starts in the dark at the fish market and ends, many hours and many small plates later, on a stool at an izakaya counter.

Set an alarm you will regret and be at the outer market by 6am, while the tuna auctions at the inner market (visible only from a viewing platform now, not the floor) are still running. The outer market's narrow lanes are for eating, not just looking: a knife-sharp slice of tamago on a stick, a bowl of uni so fresh it barely needs the rice under it, coffee poured by a vendor who has been doing this since before you were born.

By midday the crowds thin and the smart move is a nap, because the real meal starts after dark. Izakaya are not restaurants in the Western sense — you graze, you order in waves, you let the counter cook decide what's good tonight. Ask for omakase at a yakitori counter and you'll get the parts of the chicken you didn't know you wanted: knee cartilage, tail, skin grilled until it shatters.

Do at least one night in a standing bar (tachinomi) near a train station, where salarymen drink cheap sake and everyone is gone in forty minutes. It is the opposite of the reverence of the fish market and just as essential to understanding how Tokyo actually eats.
Inés Carvalho

slots.sample: Beyond the smoke and noise of the food stalls, the real lesson in Marrakech's cooking happens over a low table piled with small plates.

Jemaa el-Fnaa transforms after sunset into a food hall with no walls: dozens of numbered stalls, each shouting for your attention, serving grilled kefta skewers, snail soup ladled from a battered pot, and bowls of harira, the tomato-lentil soup that breaks the fast during Ramadan. Pick a stall that's busy with locals, not the one with the most aggressive tout.

For the fuller picture, book a meal in a riad courtyard or a family home, where dinner arrives as a spread rather than a sequence — a plate of Moroccan salads (cooked, not raw: roasted peppers, spiced carrots, aubergine zaalouk), olives, warm khobz bread, and orange slices dusted with cinnamon, all before the tagine even reaches the table.

A practical note on the tagine itself: the best ones are cooked for hours over charcoal, not gas, so don't expect fast service — a proper lamb-and-prune tagine takes as long as a slow-braised stew anywhere else, and rushing the kitchen only gets you a worse one.

slots.sample: Every October, polar bears converge on the shoreline near Churchill, Manitoba, to wait out the days until Hudson Bay freezes solid enough to hunt seals again.

The town styles itself the polar bear capital of the world, and for a few weeks each autumn that is no exaggeration — bears wander through the willow scrub in numbers found nowhere else, drawn to this exact stretch of coast by currents that freeze the bay here first. Elevated tundra buggies with viewing decks let you watch from a safe height as bears spar, doze in the low sun, or approach the vehicle out of sheer curiosity.

What surprises most visitors is how much personality comes through at close range: a mother cuffing a stubborn cub back into line, two young males play-fighting on their hind legs, the particular unhurried roll of a bear settling down to sleep on frozen ground. Temperatures swing brutally even at midday, so the buggies' heated cabins are not a luxury but a necessity.

Fly into Churchill via Winnipeg — there is no road connection — and book buggy tours well ahead, since operators cap numbers and the best late-October and early-November dates sell out a year in advance. Layer aggressively: parka, insulated boots and mitts rated well below what the forecast suggests, because wind off the bay cuts through anything less.
Mateo Duarte

slots.sample: A slow boat along Sabah's Kinabatangan River turns up more wild orangutans in an afternoon than most people see in a lifetime of nature documentaries.

The river cuts through one of the last stretches of lowland rainforest on Borneo, and its banks concentrate wildlife the way a waterhole does on the savanna. Twice a day, at dawn and again as the light goes gold before dusk, flat-bottomed boats nose along the water while guides scan the canopy for a telltale shiver of branches.

Orangutans move through the trees with a slow, deliberate grace, often a mother with an infant clinging to her flank, and it is common to drift beneath a fig tree and simply watch one feed for twenty unhurried minutes. Proboscis monkeys, hornbills and, if you are fortunate, a pygmy elephant herd wading through the shallows round out a single cruise.

Base yourself in Sukau or Bilit rather than day-tripping from Sandakan, since a lodge on the river gets you onto the water for both golden-hour cruises instead of just one. Bring a dry bag for anything electronic — afternoon squalls arrive fast and the boats have no real cover.
Hana Novak

slots.sample: A Sichuan hotpot table is a slow-motion negotiation with numbing spice, and Chengdu is where you learn to hold your own.

The classic Chengdu hotpot pot is split in two: a fiery mala broth, red with chili oil and thick with Sichuan peppercorns, and a milder white broth for anyone who needs a break. Order the divided pot even if you're confident — it lets you dial the heat up and down through the meal rather than committing to one register all night.

Ordering is done from a checklist, not a menu: thin-sliced beef and lamb, tofu skin, lotus root, quail eggs, wide rice noodles, and skewered vegetables, all destined for a few seconds in the broth. The house-made dipping sauce, usually sesame oil with garlic and cilantro, is there to cool your mouth down between bites, not to add more flavour.

Expect the peppercorns to produce a tingling numbness (ma) alongside the chili heat (la) — that combination, mala, is the whole point of Sichuan cooking, and hotpot is the most direct way to understand it. Go with a group; the pot is built for sharing, and the ritual of fishing things out together is half the meal.
Mateo Duarte

slots.sample: Between a simit cart in Europe and a fish sandwich in Asia lies the most efficient food tour in the world — a twenty-minute ferry ride.

Start on the European side in Karaköy, where fishermen sell their catch straight off the boats by the Galata Bridge and simit sellers push red carts stacked with sesame-crusted rings of bread still warm from the oven. Eat one plain, standing up, the way everyone else is — it's breakfast, not a snack.

Work your way through Kadıköy market on the Asian side for the things a menu can't capture: a wedge of lor cheese from a stall that's sold nothing else for thirty years, wet walnuts pickled in syrup, stuffed mussels (midye dolma) sold from a tray balanced on one arm. Wash it all down with a glass of tea poured from a samovar that never stops boiling.

For dinner, find a meyhane — Istanbul's answer to a tapas bar — and let the waiter walk you through a tray of cold mezze before the grilled fish arrives. Order rakı, the anise spirit that turns cloudy with water, and pace yourself; a proper meyhane meal runs three hours and several courses longer than you plan for.

slots.sample: Seoul's oldest covered market is where grandmothers who've run the same stall for forty years still out-cook every trendy restaurant in the city.

Gwangjang has been open since 1905, and its food alley runs on a system that hasn't changed much since: pick a stall, sit on the plastic stool, and order by pointing, because the ajummas running the pans are too busy to explain the menu twice. Bindaetteok — thick mung bean pancakes fried on flat griddles until the edges crisp — is the market's signature dish, and the smoke and sizzle of a dozen pans going at once is half the reason people come.

Work through the alley methodically: mayak gimbap (tiny 'addictive' seaweed rice rolls, dipped in mustard sauce), knife-cut noodles in a spicy broth, and yukhoe, Korean beef tartare mixed with pear and egg yolk at a stall that's sold nothing else for generations. Everything is cheap by design — this is a market for eating a lot of small things, not one large meal.

Go at night when the stalls are lit with bare bulbs and the steam off the pans catches the light — it's louder, more crowded, and considerably more fun than a daytime visit, though if raw beef isn't your thing, an afternoon trip still delivers on the pancakes and noodles alone.
Priscila Rocha

slots.sample: The 150-kilometre loop around Mount Rainier crosses more vertical gain than the Grand Canyon rim-to-rim, one river valley and ridge at a time.

I permitted the trip through the lottery system months ahead, since Wonderland Trail camps are capped and highly competitive for the short July-to-September window when the high passes are reliably clear of snow. The trail circles Rainier at a near-constant middle distance, so the mountain itself is almost always visible, but the terrain underfoot changes completely every few hours — old-growth forest, subalpine meadow, glacial river crossing, scree.

Panhandle Gap, the trail's highest point, still held snow patches when I crossed in early August, and the view stretched south to Mount Adams and, on a clear day, Mount St Helens beyond it. River crossings are the trip's real hazard rather than altitude — the Tahoma and Carbon rivers run high with glacial melt on hot afternoons, and rangers recommend crossing them as early in the day as your itinerary allows.

I carried a bear canister as required and had one uneventful but memorable evening watching a black bear work a huckleberry patch across the valley from camp. Split the trip into ten or eleven days rather than the aggressive seven some parties attempt — the elevation gain adds up fast, and Rainier's weather can close in with little warning even in August.
Yuki Tanabe

slots.sample: Between Chamonix and Zermatt lie two weeks, six high passes, and views of the Mont Blanc massif and the Matterhorn from opposite ends of the same walk.

I split the route into eleven stages and stayed in a mix of refuges and small village hotels, the usual compromise between the ski-touring version's mountain huts and a gentler summer itinerary. The high point is the Col de Riedmatten above Arolla, a scramble up fixed cables and scree most guidebooks undersell, followed by a long descent into a valley that feels emptied of everyone but marmots.

Cabane de Prafleuri and Cabane des Dix both sit in genuinely wild terrain, glacial and grey, a hard contrast to the flower meadows around Champex-Lac a few days earlier. The Swiss huts serve dinner at a fixed hour and expect payment in cash, so I carried more francs than felt sensible for a hiking trip.

The last two days into Zermatt trade solitude for crowds as you join day-trippers from the Gornergrat, but the payoff is real: the Matterhorn appears and reappears around every ridge for the final thirty kilometres. Go in the first half of September if you can — the passes are usually clear of new snow and the huts have thinned out from the August rush.
Omar Benali

slots.sample: The knife-edge above two impossibly blue lakes is Norway's most photographed day hike, and it earns every one of its warnings.

I based myself at the Gjendesheim lodge on the shore of Lake Gjende and caught the first boat across to Memurubu, which is how almost everyone tackles Besseggen — the ridge is far harder walked the other direction. From Memurubu the trail climbs fast through scree to the saddle below Besshø, and for a long, exposed stretch you're balanced on a ridge with Lake Bessvatnet dropping turquoise on one side and Gjende a darker blue nearly four hundred metres below on the other.

The scramble sections aren't technical, but they're airy enough that I stopped noticing the cold and started noticing my hands on the rock instead. Cloud rolls in off the Jotunheimen peaks with little warning, and I met a Norwegian guide who turns back parties the moment visibility drops below the next cairn.

Do it as a long day from Gjendesheim rather than trying to add huts — the DNT cabins nearby are better used before or after for the wider Jotunheimen network, with Glitterheim and Memurubu both good bookends. Go in August; the snow patches that linger into July make the ridge crossing considerably more serious.
Freya Lindqvist

slots.sample: An hour's flight from Ibiza's clubs, Menorca keeps its coastline the way the Balearics looked before mass tourism arrived.

The island's calas — narrow limestone inlets with a sliver of sand at the end — are strung along both coasts, and a UNESCO Biosphere designation has kept most of them free of the sunbed rows and beach clubs that define its neighbors; Cala Macarella and Cala Turqueta draw the most visitors, so arrive by nine or hike in via the Camí de Cavalls coastal path instead.

That path, a 185-kilometer route that once moved horses and troops between garrisons, is today the best way to reach coves with no road access at all — pack water, since the calas themselves have little shade and no facilities.

Menorca's south-coast beaches face the swimming-pool-calm Mediterranean, while the north coast, wilder and rockier, takes the brunt of the tramuntana wind; choose your coast based on the forecast, and you can usually find a sheltered cala somewhere on the island even on a blustery day.

slots.sample: The Seychelles' inner islands are built from granite, not coral, and the boulders piled on their beaches are unlike anything else in the Indian Ocean.

La Digue's Anse Source d'Argent is the most photographed beach in the Seychelles for good reason — house-sized granite boulders, rounded by millennia of surf, frame small pools of impossibly clear water; go at opening time or in the last hour before closing to have stretches of it to yourself.

The island runs on bicycles rather than cars, which makes it easy to string together several beaches in a day — Grand Anse and Petite Anse to the south are wilder and less sheltered, better for watching waves break than for swimming.

Praslin, a short ferry away, holds the Vallée de Mai, a UNESCO-listed palm forest that backs directly onto Anse Lazio, arguably the finest swimming beach in the archipelago; pair a forest walk with an afternoon swim and you've covered the two faces of these islands in a single day.
Yuki Tanabe

slots.sample: Off the western tip of New Guinea, Raja Ampat's scattered limestone islands sit above the richest marine biodiversity on Earth.

The classic view — jungled karst islands poking out of turquoise water, best seen from the viewpoint above Piaynemo — barely hints at what's underwater; the archipelago's reefs hold more coral and fish species than anywhere else surveyed, and even a short snorkel off a homestay jetty turns up reef sharks and turtles.

Homestays, simple wooden bungalows built and run by local families on islands like Kri and Arborek, are how most travelers experience Raja Ampat, and staying in one channels tourism money directly to the communities managing the marine protected areas that keep the reefs healthy.

Getting here takes effort — a flight to Sorong followed by a public or chartered boat to the islands — and that friction is part of what has kept Raja Ampat wild; budget several days beyond the travel itself, since bad weather can delay boat transfers without warning.
Hana Novak

slots.sample: A narrow-gauge steam-era line squeezes between shopfronts and switchbacks its way up nearly two thousand metres to the tea town of Darjeeling.

The track is barely wider than a garden path — two feet, to be exact — and for long stretches it runs directly down the middle of the Hill Cart Road, so your train shares space with taxis, pedestrians and the occasional cow between New Jalpaiguri and Darjeeling. It has done this since 1881, and UNESCO now protects it as a working World Heritage Site rather than a museum piece.

The signature stretch is the Batasia Loop, where the line spirals over itself to lose height gently enough for the little engines to manage, framing a war memorial with a panorama of Kangchenjunga on a clear morning. Further down, the Agony Point switchback earns its name honestly — the driver reverses the whole train around a hairpin too tight for a normal curve.

Most travellers ride the shorter joyride service from Darjeeling to Ghum, the highest railway station in India, rather than the full seven-hour haul from the plains — it's enough to get the tea-garden views, the diesel-and-steam smell of the old locomotives, and the strange intimacy of a train passing so close to shopfronts you could touch the awnings.

Book the steam-hauled joyride specifically if you can; several services now run modern diesel units instead, which move faster but lose the theatre. Bring a scarf even in summer — Darjeeling sits high enough that mornings stay properly cold.
Yuki Tanabe

slots.sample: Often voted the world's most scenic railway, this line from Fort William to Mallaig crosses lochs, moor and one very famous curved viaduct.

The regular ScotRail service already justifies the trip on its own — Rannoch Moor's bog and heather stretching to the horizon, Loch Eilt's small wooded islands, the sudden reveal of the sea at Arisaig. But most people come for one specific ninety seconds: the curve of the Glenfinnan Viaduct, twenty-one arches sweeping in a long stone bow above the glen, best known now as the bridge the Hogwarts Express crosses in the Harry Potter films.

You can ride it on the ordinary diurnal train for a fraction of the cost, or take the Jacobite steam service that runs the same route in summer, trailing smoke over the viaduct for the photographers gathered on the hillside viewpoint above Glenfinnan station. Either way, sit on the left heading toward Mallaig for the water views along Loch Shiel and the coast.

Mallaig itself is a working fishing port rather than a tourist set piece — arrive hungry and eat whatever came off the boats that morning, then catch the ferry across to Skye if you want to keep the journey going by water instead of rail.

The full line runs from Glasgow, but the Fort William to Mallaig leg is the concentrated highlight — about ninety minutes each way. Book the Jacobite well ahead in July and August; it sells out weeks in advance.
Priscila Rocha

slots.sample: Named for the Afghan cameleers who once opened this route, the Ghan crosses an entire continent from Adelaide to Darwin through country few travellers ever see.

The journey covers nearly three thousand kilometres of the emptiest interior on the planet — scrub, then desert, then the sudden deep red of the Simpson Desert's dune country, then finally tropical green as you approach the Top End. Old rusted locomotives and abandoned sidings from the original narrow-gauge line still sit out in the desert near towns like Marree, remnants of the route's much harder early history before the modern standard-gauge line replaced it in 2004.

Off-train excursions are built into the ticket and are where the trip really opens up: a sunset walk through the West MacDonnell Ranges outside Alice Springs, a visit to Katherine Gorge further north, or simply time in the small town of Alice Springs itself, roughly the halfway point and the only real settlement the route passes through for hundreds of kilometres in either direction.

Onboard, the days settle into a rhythm of dining car meals, a lounge car with a well-stocked bar, and long unbroken hours watching country scroll past that changes almost imperceptibly hour to hour but transforms completely over the length of the journey. Cabins are small but proper beds, not couchettes, which matters over three days.

Book well ahead — the Ghan operates on a fixed seasonal schedule rather than daily departures, running more frequently between April and November. The heat further north can be extreme even in the shoulder months, so factor that into what you pack for the excursions.
Priscila Rocha

slots.sample: Nothing in East Africa matches the noise and nerve of a wildebeest column throwing itself into the crocodile-thick Mara River at the height of the migration.

By late July the herds have massed on the Serengeti bank in their thousands, bellowing and pacing for hours before a single animal finally commits. Once the first wildebeest goes, the whole column follows in a scrambling, dust-choked rush, hooves drumming on mud and rock as zebras thread through the chaos alongside them.

The crossing itself lasts only minutes but it is total sensory overload: the crack of horns against horns, the slap of bodies hitting water, a crocodile surfacing exactly where you did not expect one. Guides cut the engine and let the vehicle drift into position well before the herd commits, because once it starts there is no repositioning without spooking the animals mid-crossing.

Base yourself on the Kenyan side of the Mara Triangle or the northern Serengeti between late July and September, when the migration is most likely to be pinned against the river. Pack a long lens and patience in equal measure — some mornings you wait four hours for a crossing that never comes, and that is simply the honest rhythm of following a wild herd.
Mateo Duarte

Blue feet and no fear: wildlife encounters in the Galápagos

slots.sample: From the postcard valley of Kamikochi, a two-day scramble leads to the sharpest summit in Japan's Northern Alps.

Kamikochi itself is almost too civilised to be a trailhead — a valley of clear glacial water and larch forest reachable only by bus, closed to private cars, and busy with day-trippers photographing the Azusa River. I left most of them behind within the first hour, following the river upstream through beech forest before the real climbing starts toward Yarisawa hut.

The final push to Yarigatake's summit is where the trip earns its reputation: a scramble up iron ladders and chains bolted into near-vertical rock, exposed enough that I was glad of the queue slowing everyone to single file at the crux. Mountain huts here run like small hotels, with futons, hot meals and beer for sale, which makes the Japan Alps a strange, comfortable version of high-altitude trekking.

Yarigatake's summit is small and often crowded at sunrise, so I got there the evening before instead and had the ridge nearly to myself. Reserve hut space ahead in peak season, late July to August — Japanese hiking holidays fill Yarisawa and Yarigatake-sanso lodges fast, and turning up without a booking means a long walk back down in the dark.

slots.sample: Twenty kilometres of switchbacks and waterfalls connect the fjord village of Flåm to the high mountain junction at Myrdal.

The Flåmsbana climbs 866 metres in under twenty kilometres, a gradient steep enough that the line needed five separate reversing tunnels blasted through solid rock to manage it without switchbacks on the surface. From the fjord-level village of Flåm the train winds up through farmland, then birch forest, then bare mountain, crossing the same valley on different levels so many times that you lose count.

The set-piece stop is Kjosfossen, a thundering waterfall where the train pauses for a few minutes so passengers can get out onto a viewing platform right beside the falls, close enough to feel the spray. In summer a red-clad figure sometimes appears on the rocks above — a nod to local folklore about the huldra, the forest spirits said to lure travellers with song.

At the top, Myrdal connects to the main Oslo–Bergen line, which means you can build a full day out of it: ride the Bergen Railway across the high Hardangervidda plateau, change at Myrdal, and descend the Flåm branch to sea level before catching a fjord cruise onward from the village itself.

Sit on the right-hand side heading down toward Flåm for the best waterfall and valley views. The full descent takes about an hour, and even in July the higher sections can be genuinely cold — pack a proper layer, not just a cardigan.
Kwame Mensah

slots.sample: North of the Arctic Circle, Lofoten's beaches sit beneath jagged granite peaks, and in summer the sun barely sets on them.

Kvalvika and Haukland look tropical in photographs — white sand, turquoise shallows — until you feel the water, which stays close to freezing even in July; the payoff is a beach framed by sheer mountains rising straight out of the sand, with not a palm tree in sight.

Kvalvika has no road access — you park near Fredvang and walk forty minutes over a low pass, which keeps the crowds thin even in peak season; Haukland and neighboring Uttakleiv are roadside and busier, but both stay free and open all night under the midnight sun from late May to mid-July.

Bring a wetsuit if you actually want to swim rather than just wade, and a stove for coffee — Lofoten rewards those who linger past the day-trip window, when the light turns gold around what would be midnight anywhere else.

slots.sample: The Pantanal's flooded rivers hold the best odds on Earth of watching a wild jaguar hunt in daylight, from the low seat of a skiff.

Unlike the Amazon's dense canopy, the Pantanal's open wetlands and clear sightlines mean jaguars here hunt caiman and capybara along exposed riverbanks in full view of a boat. Spotters radio between skiffs along the Rio Cuiabá and Três Irmãos, so a sighting anywhere on the water usually pulls two or three boats into a respectful, engine-off arc within minutes.

You come to recognise the tells before the cat itself appears: a line of birds lifting off a bank in alarm, capybara freezing mid-graze, or simply your guide cutting speed and pointing at a patch of shade that looks, at first, like nothing at all. When a jaguar does step down to drink, it moves with an unhurried confidence that makes the whole boatload go silent at once.

Go in the dry season, June through October, when falling water levels concentrate prey and cats alike along the exposed banks and the dirt access road, the Transpantaneira, is passable end to end. Stay at a fazenda lodge with its own boats rather than a day-tripping operator — the earlier starts and later returns are where the best sightings happen.
Omar Benali

slots.sample: Toronto to Vancouver by transcontinental train trades speed for a slow unspooling of prairie, mountain and lake that no highway or flight can match.

The Canadian leaves Toronto's Union Station and doesn't really stop being impressive until it reaches the Pacific four days later. The first stretch through Northern Ontario is granite and black spruce and lake after lake, the Canadian Shield at its most repetitive and most hypnotic — you start to understand why this landscape produced a whole school of painters obsessed with exactly this scenery.

Day two brings the Prairies, and this is where the train's slowness becomes the whole point: hour after hour of wheat and canola under a sky too big for any window to properly frame, grain elevators marking small towns from a great distance before the train ever reaches them. The dome cars — glass-topped observation carriages — are worth the upgrade here if nowhere else on the trip.

Then the Rockies arrive almost without warning outside Jasper, and the last day is spent winding through mountain passes and river gorges toward the coast, the scenery changing register completely from the plains. Meals in the dining car are included in sleeper class and run on a fixed schedule that becomes its own kind of ritual — you eat when the train says to eat, and you meet whoever is seated across from you.

Book a cabin rather than coach if your budget allows; four days sitting upright adds up. And bring patience for delays — this is a passenger train sharing freight track, and schedules are treated as more of a suggestion the further west you go.
Mateo Duarte

slots.sample: The Okavango Delta is a rare inland river that never reaches the sea, and the quietest way to experience it is from a hand-poled mokoro sliding silently between the reeds.

Water flooding down from Angolan highlands spreads across the Kalahari sands each year, transforming dry bush into a maze of lagoons and channels that draws game from across northern Botswana. A mokoro poler standing at the stern reads the water with a practised eye, easing the canoe past lily pads and papyrus with barely a ripple, so animals rarely register your approach until you are already close.

Elephants wade and swim between islands with only trunks and backs breaking the surface, hippos surface and submerge in the deeper channels, and red lechwe bound through the shallows in explosive leaps when startled. The silence of a mokoro compared to a vehicle changes the whole texture of a sighting — you hear the water move before you see what caused it.

The flood typically peaks between June and August, when water levels are highest and mokoro access opens up further into the delta's interior; drier months favour game drives instead as channels shrink. Choose a camp with both mokoro and vehicle safaris on offer so you are not locked into one mode of travel regardless of that week's water levels.
Priscila Rocha

slots.sample: Between Positano and Ravello, a handful of small hotels are terraced directly into the limestone cliffs, close enough to the drop that the Tyrrhenian Sea seems to start at your balcony rail.

These properties are built the way the coast itself is built — in switchbacks and staircases, room by room down a cliff face wrapped in bougainvillea and lemon terraces. Because the road arrives at the top, many hotels run a private lift or a long stone stairway down to their own sun deck and swimming platform, so ask about the descent before you book if stairs are a concern.

Rooms are usually small and simply finished with handmade majolica tile floors and iron balconies, because the view is the real amenity: sheer blue water, fishing boats, and at night the lit-up towns strung along the coastline like a necklace. A rooftop or terrace restaurant is often the best table on the property, worth booking for dinner even if you eat elsewhere the rest of the trip.

Reserve a sea-facing room rather than the cheaper garden or hillside category — on a coast this narrow, the difference in outlook is enormous — and travel light, since porters still carry bags down real steps at most of these places.

slots.sample: Four days of dense Sierra Nevada jungle lead to more than a thousand stone terraces built by the Tayrona centuries before the Spanish arrived.

The trek starts outside Santa Marta and follows the Buritaca River valley through a humidity that never really lets up, crossing the river itself a dozen times on foot and by cable pulley when it's running high. I stayed in open-sided hammock camps each night, mosquito nets included, sharing meals with the same small group of trekkers and indigenous guides for the full four days.

The Kogi and Wiwa communities who still live in the valley are the trek's other half of the story — thatched-roof villages appear along the route, and the guides, several of them Kogi themselves, explain the site's spiritual weight to their own people rather than treating it as a ruin. Ciudad Perdida itself is reached by twelve hundred stone steps cut into the hillside, still slick with moss when I climbed them just after dawn to beat the day-trip crowds arriving by helicopter.

Pack for both heat and rain regardless of season — the valley generates its own weather most afternoons — and bring cash, since there's nowhere to draw money once you leave Santa Marta. Only a handful of licensed agencies run the trek, all following the same route and price band by agreement with the local communities, so choose based on group size rather than itinerary.
Kwame Mensah

slots.sample: On Scotland's Atlantic edge, the Outer Hebrides hide beaches so pale and so empty that photos of them are routinely mistaken for the Caribbean.

Luskentyre, on the Isle of Harris, is the headline beach — three miles of blinding white machair sand backed by grazing sheep and the Harris hills, with turquoise shallows that owe their color to crushed shell rather than warmth; the water rarely climbs out of the mid-teens Celsius even in August.

The chain's beaches are strung along the west coasts of Lewis, Harris, and the Uists, connected by a single winding road and a series of causeways and ferries, so a beach-hopping road trip here means slow going and constant weather changes — pack for all four seasons in one afternoon.

Go for the light rather than the swimming: early morning or evening sun turns the machair grass gold and the sand near-luminous, and with so few visitors reaching this far northwest, you'll often have an entire bay to yourself.

slots.sample: In the Basque country's food capital, dinner means a slow walk through the old town, one small plate and one glass of txakoli at a time.

The Parte Vieja crams dozens of pintxos bars into a few blocks, each with a counter piled high with skewered bites — anchovy and pepper, tortilla wedges, seared foie gras on bread. The etiquette is simple: order one or two pintxos and a glass, eat standing at the bar or on the street, then move on to the next place. Nobody stays for a full meal in one spot.

Some bars are famous for a single dish, and it's worth crossing town for it: a gilda (the original pintxo, a skewer of anchovy, olive, and guindilla pepper), a mushroom pintxo grilled to order, a warm croqueta that shatters on the first bite. Keep a mental tally of your toothpicks — that's how the bill gets calculated at the end.

Go early evening to catch the first wave before it gets three-deep at the bar, and save one night for a sit-down meal at a sidrería in the hills above town, where cider is poured from height and the only choices are steak, cod omelette, and how much you can eat.
Priscila Rocha

slots.sample: A loop through Berber villages and high scree slopes in Morocco's High Atlas ends atop North Africa's tallest peak.

I hired a mule and a guide in Imlil, the trailhead village an hour from Marrakech, which is standard practice here and cheap enough that almost every trekker does the same. The circuit climbs through walnut groves and irrigated terraces before the villages thin out and the trail turns to bare scree above Sidi Chamharouch, a small shrine marking the last real settlement before the mountains close in.

Refuge du Toubkal sits at the base of the final ascent, a functional stone building crowded with trekkers timing their summit push for sunrise. The push to the top of Jbel Toubkal at 4,167 metres is a long, unglamorous scree slog rather than a technical climb, but the altitude and the pre-dawn cold make it feel harder than the numbers suggest.

I came down via the Tizi n'Ougdemt pass rather than retracing my steps, a longer route into the Azzaden valley that trades crowds for empty ridgelines and a last night in a Berber guesthouse. Go in late spring or early autumn — midsummer heat in the lower valleys is brutal, and winter turns the summit push into a genuine mountaineering objective requiring crampons.
Omar Benali

slots.sample: Between El Nido and Coron, a scatter of limestone islands hides lagoons so still they barely register as water.

El Nido's Bacuit archipelago is the famous half — karst towers dropping straight into turquoise water, accessible mostly by the standardized island-hopping tours that every outfitter in town runs; book Tour A for the Big and Small Lagoons, and go early, before the boats stack up at the lagoon mouths.

Coron, a few hours north by ferry, trades lagoons for wrecks — a dozen Japanese ships sunk here in 1944 sit in clear, shallow water and are snorkelable without a certification, alongside Kayangan Lake, routinely ranked the cleanest lake in the Philippines and reached by a short, steep climb over limestone.

Skip the group boats when you can and hire a private bangka for a half-day; it costs more, but it means reaching Secret Lagoon or Twin Lagoon before the flotillas arrive, and the boatmen know which coves the standard tours skip entirely.

slots.sample: In Italy's food capital, the best meals start with flour on the counter and a nonna correcting your technique.

Bologna doesn't do tourist pasta. Book a morning with a sfoglina — a pasta maker, almost always a woman, almost always self-taught from watching her own mother — in a kitchen behind an unmarked door near Via Pescherie Vecchie. You'll crack eggs into a flour well, work the dough until your forearms ache, and roll it thinner than you thought possible before it goes under the knife for tagliatelle.

What you make in the morning you eat in the afternoon, usually with a ragù that has been reducing since before you arrived — real Bolognese is a slow, meat-heavy sauce, barely tomato at all, nothing like the red sludge sold under its name elsewhere. Order it at a trattoria on a side street rather than the piazza-facing places, and expect a short menu that hasn't changed in decades.

Save room for tortellini in brodo, the dish locals actually crave on a cold night: tiny meat-filled pasta swimming in clear capon broth. A market stall in Quadrilatero, the medieval food quarter, will sell you a kilo of fresh tortellini to take home — vacuum it before your flight and it survives the trip better than any souvenir.
Mateo Duarte

slots.sample: South America's only luxury sleeper train climbs out of the Sacred Valley and across the high Andean plateau to Puno on Lake Titicaca.

The route leaves Cusco and climbs almost immediately, threading through farming villages where llamas graze alongside the tracks and adobe houses give way to increasingly bare, high-altitude terrain. By the time you reach La Raya pass, you're above 4,300 metres — higher than most Alpine summits — with jagged brown peaks filling the windows and thin cold air that the pressurised carriages handle so smoothly you barely notice.

Meals are served in a dining car with white tablecloths and small lamps at every table, a genuinely incongruous dose of formality against the raw altiplano scenery sliding past outside. There's a piano bar carriage and an open-air observation car at the rear for photographs — worth braving the cold and thin air for, especially as the light goes gold in late afternoon.

The journey ends at Puno on the shore of Lake Titicaca, the highest large navigable lake in the world, where reed islands built by the Uros people float just offshore — a possible extension if you have another day to spare before heading back toward Cusco or on to Bolivia.

The full one-way trip takes about ten hours, so pace yourself with the wine list and the altitude both — even seasoned travellers feel La Raya's thin air. Bring sunglasses; the plateau light at four thousand metres is fierce even through glass.
Freya Lindqvist

slots.sample: Get invited to a Georgian supra and you'll understand why the country calls its feast table a small government, complete with its own elected leader.

A proper supra is run by a tamada, a toastmaster chosen for wit and stamina, who paces the meal through a long sequence of toasts — to peace, to ancestors, to the guests, to love — each one drunk in full from a horn or a clay cup of local wine. You don't clink glasses in Georgia; you wait for the toast to land, then drink.

The food arrives all at once and keeps arriving: khachapuri, the cheese-filled bread that comes in a dozen regional shapes, from the boat-shaped Adjaruli topped with a raw egg to the round Imeruli; khinkali, soup-filled dumplings you're meant to eat by hand, sipping the broth through a bite before finishing the rest; and pkhali, walnut-and-vegetable pâtés that turn up in more colours than you'd expect from beets, spinach, and leeks.

Tbilisi's old town has restaurants that recreate the supra format for visitors, but if a local invites you to a real one, go — it runs for hours, involves more wine than seems reasonable on a weeknight, and is the single best way to understand Georgian hospitality from the inside.
Hana Novak
A Pho Crawl Through Hanoi's Old Quarter

slots.sample: A volcanic outcrop 350 kilometers off Brazil's northeast coast, Fernando de Noronha limits its own visitor numbers to protect the reason people come.

Baía do Sancho, reached by a ladder bolted into a cliff crevice, tops most rankings of Brazil's best beach, and for once the ranking holds up — turtles and reef fish are visible from the shallows without a mask, and the cliffs framing it block most of the wind.

Brazil caps the number of tourists allowed on the island at any time and charges a daily environmental preservation tax on top of park entry fees, which keeps Noronha expensive and uncrowded by Brazilian-coast standards; book accommodation and the tax registration well before you fly in from Recife or Natal.

Spinner dolphins gather by the hundreds in the Baía dos Golfinhos most mornings, a ritual best watched from the clifftop trail above rather than the water, since the bay itself is protected from swimmers to keep the pod undisturbed.
Yuki Tanabe

slots.sample: Nepal's original teahouse trek circles the Annapurna massif over three weeks and one genuinely high pass at 5,416 metres.

I started in Besisahar and spent the first week gaining altitude gently through Manang district's pine forests and terraced barley fields, sleeping in teahouses that get simpler and colder the higher you climb. By Manang, at 3,500 metres, most groups take a mandatory acclimatisation day, and I used mine to hike up to the Gangapurna glacier viewpoint rather than rest in the lodge.

Thorong La itself is a long, cold, unglamorous slog — a 3am start from High Camp, crampon-worthy ice in places after fresh snow, and a summit that's really just the start of the knee-jarring descent to Muktinath on the other side. What stayed with me was the change in landscape rather than the pass: the wet, green Marsyangdi valley on the eastern approach gives way completely to the high desert of Mustang on the way down.

Buy a walking pole locally in Besisahar or Kathmandu rather than pack one — it's one less thing to carry on the flight, and every teahouse town sells them. Budget more days than the circuit technically requires; altitude sickness sends more trekkers home early than any other single cause, and Manang's acclimatisation day is not optional no matter how good you feel.
Kwame Mensah

slots.sample: In Göreme, entire hotel rooms are hand-carved from soft volcanic rock, and waking inside one feels less like a hotel stay than borrowing a piece of geology for the night.

The best cave hotels in Göreme and neighboring Uçhisar are not decorated to look like caves — they are caves, tunneled generations ago into the region's soft tuff stone and only recently fitted with plumbing and underfloor heating. Walls run a meter thick, curving into vaulted ceilings and stone alcoves that double as headboards, shelves and window seats without a single nail.

That thickness keeps the rooms remarkably cool through the valley's hot afternoons and warm once the sun drops, and the silence inside is total — no street noise reaches through solid rock. Most properties are stacked up a hillside, so your terrace looks straight out over a jumble of fairy chimneys and, if you are up early enough, dozens of hot-air balloons lifting off in the pink pre-dawn light.

Pay a little more for a room with its own private terrace rather than a shared one, and ask specifically whether the room is an original excavated cave or a newer concrete-and-stone build made to match — both can be lovely, but only one gives you the real thick-walled hush that makes the stay worth it.
Inés Carvalho

slots.sample: Yala holds one of the highest densities of leopards anywhere on the planet, and unlike most big-cat destinations, here the odds of a sighting genuinely favour you.

The park's dry scrub and rocky outcrops give leopards clear vantage points to survey their territory, and with no larger predator to compete against, they hunt and rest in the open with a confidence rarely seen elsewhere. A jeep convoy easing to a stop, radios crackling between drivers, is usually the first sign that a cat has been spotted lounging on a boulder or padding along a trail.

What makes Yala's leopards so watchable is their sheer indifference to vehicles — a cat will often walk straight past a line of jeeps, close enough to see the individual rosettes in its coat, without breaking stride. Elephants, sloth bears and a huge diversity of waterbirds fill the gaps between leopard sightings, so even a quiet game drive rarely feels empty.

Block 1, nearest the entrance, has the highest leopard density but also the heaviest jeep traffic in peak season; consider Block 5 or a private reserve on the park's boundary for a quieter, less crowded safari. Visit in the dry season from February to July, when receding waterholes concentrate both predators and prey along predictable routes.
Kwame Mensah

slots.sample: Lisbon is a city built on seven hills, and the trams exist for exactly that reason.

Ride the number 28 tram end to end at least once, ideally early, before the queue for a seat stretches around the block. It rattles through the Alfama's narrow lanes close enough to touch the tiled facades on either side — the best free sightseeing tour the city offers.

Spend a morning getting lost in the Alfama itself on foot, fado drifting out of doorways, then climb to the Miradouro da Senhora do Monte for the widest view over the rooftops down to the Tejo river. Lunch on grilled sardines and a glass of vinho verde somewhere with no view at all — the food is usually better where the tourists are not looking.

Cross to Belem for the custard tarts at the original Pasteis de Belem bakery, still warm and dusted with cinnamon, and the Jeronimos Monastery next door. Close the weekend at a miradouro at sunset with a glass of ginjinha, the sour cherry liqueur sold from tiny hatches all over the old town — Lisbon does its best work in that last hour of light.

slots.sample: The resplendent quetzal's iridescent tail and improbable colouring have drawn birders to Costa Rica's high cloud forest for decades, and the valley of San Gerardo de Dota remains the surest place to find one.

At nearly 2,300 metres in the Talamanca mountains, the air turns cool and the forest closes into a dripping tangle of oaks draped in moss and bromeliads. Quetzals nest in these hollow oak trunks and feed on wild avocado, so local guides know the fruiting trees by heart and can often position a group beneath one before the bird even shows.

The reveal, when it comes, still stops conversation: a flash of iridescent green and crimson, then that absurdly long tail streaming behind as the bird settles on a branch to swallow a fruit whole. Mixed flocks of tanagers and trogons move through the same canopy, so the wait between quetzal sightings is rarely dull.

Go between January and April, the local dry season and also nesting time, when quetzals are most reliably active around their chosen trees in the early morning. Book a guide the evening before rather than wandering alone — their knowledge of which specific tree is fruiting that week is the difference between an hour's wait and a full morning's search.
Omar Benali

slots.sample: Sri Lanka's hill-country line climbs through terraced tea gardens and over the famous Nine Arch Bridge on its way to the cool town of Ella.

The train from Kandy climbs almost from the first mile, leaving the humid lowlands behind for a cooler, greener world of tea estates that carpet every hillside in tight, geometric rows. Pickers in bright saris move between the bushes as the train passes, and the smell of processing sheds drifts through open windows at stations like Nanu Oya, the stop for Nuwara Eliya.

Doors are left open for the whole ride, which is technically against the rules and practically the entire point — passengers lean out or sit in the doorway with legs dangling as the carriages sway through curve after curve. Second and third class are where the real atmosphere lives; the reserved first-class observation car is comfortable but oddly sealed off from the experience everyone comes for.

The line's postcard moment is the Nine Arch Bridge outside Ella, a colonial-era viaduct built without steel — legend says its engineer used only brick, cement and railway track after wartime steel shortages — now framed by jungle and tea slopes on every side. Get off a stop early at Demodara and walk to the bridge for photos before continuing on to Ella itself.

Book second class in advance through the official reservation system if you want a guaranteed seat — this route has become popular enough that unreserved carriages fill early. The full Kandy–Ella run takes six to seven hours; treat it as the destination, not the commute.
Yuki Tanabe

slots.sample: Kyoto's narrow wooden merchant townhouses, once slated for demolition by the hundred, are now some of the city's most sought-after places to sleep.

A machiya is built long and thin — 'the bed of an eel,' locals call the shape — running back from a slim street frontage through a series of tatami rooms toward a small tsuboniwa courtyard garden at the rear. Restorations keep the sliding shoji screens, the dark timber beams and the low doorways, while quietly adding underfloor heating, modern plumbing and soundproofing between rooms.

Days here start with shoes off at the genkan entryway and often end sitting on the engawa veranda looking at the courtyard garden, which is lit at night for exactly this purpose. Most machiya are self-contained rentals rather than staffed hotels, so you get an entire townhouse to yourselves — genuinely quiet, and a five- or ten-minute walk from the lantern-lit lanes of Gion or Pontocho.

Book one within easy walking distance of Gion if evening strolls matter to you, and check in advance whether the beds are futons on tatami or a Western-style frame — machiya vary, and futons are part of the experience for some travelers and a dealbreaker for others.
Hana Novak

slots.sample: On Zanzibar's northeast coast, dhows still outnumber jet skis, and the real tidal rhythm of the Indian Ocean sets the pace of the day.

Most visitors land at Nungwi or Kendwa, the island's postcard strip of white sand and sunset bars, but the coast keeps going — south past Matemwe's seaweed farms and on to the quieter villages around Pongwe and Michamvi, where the sand is just as fine and the crowds thin to nothing.

Zanzibar's tides swing hard, sometimes three or four meters, so a beach that's lapping at your towel at noon can be a half-mile walk to open water by four; plan swims around the tide chart rather than the clock, and use the low-tide hours to wade out and watch the seaweed farmers working by hand.

Stay in a small guesthouse rather than an all-inclusive resort and you'll eat better for less — grilled octopus and Zanzibar mix from a beachfront stall beats any buffet, and the money stays on the island.

slots.sample: Off West Africa, Cabo Verde's desert islands trade lush greenery for wind, wide-open sand, and some of the Atlantic's best kitesurfing.

Sal's Praia de Santa Maria is the archipelago's best-known stretch — a long, gently sloping beach where local fishermen still haul in their catch at the pier each morning, right alongside the kite schools that have made the island a windsports destination.

Boa Vista, a short flight away, is emptier and more dramatic — Praia de Chaves and Praia de Cabral run for kilometers of undeveloped dune, and loggerhead turtles nest on several beaches between June and October, with licensed guides running respectful night walks to watch them.

Pack layers even for a beach trip — the harmattan wind off the Sahara keeps temperatures pleasant but can turn a calm morning gusty by afternoon, which is exactly what draws the kitesurfers here in the first place.

slots.sample: In Lima, ceviche is a lunchtime ritual with rules — eaten fresh, eaten early, and never after dark.

Peruvian ceviche is built on leche de tigre, the citrus-and-chili marinade that 'cooks' raw fish in minutes, and the best cebicherías only serve it at lunch, when the fish market delivery is hours old rather than a full day. Arrive by 1pm; some of Lima's most respected spots close once the day's catch runs out, sometimes before 3pm.

Order the classic first — corvina or another firm white fish, cut into clean cubes, dressed table-side so the citrus doesn't over-cure it, served with sweet potato and toasted corn (cancha) to cut the acidity. Then branch out: tiradito, ceviche's Nikkei cousin, sliced sashimi-thin under a different sauce, reflects Lima's century-old Japanese-Peruvian food tradition as clearly as any dish in the city.

A cebichería is not a fine-dining occasion even when the plating is elegant — expect plastic chairs alongside white tablecloths, a short beer list, and a leche de tigre shot offered on the house once your plate is clean. Drink it; it's considered both a digestif and a hangover cure, and turning it down is a small missed rite of passage.
Yuki Tanabe

slots.sample: Kaziranga's tall elephant grass and Brahmaputra floodplain hold two-thirds of the world's greater one-horned rhinos, a conservation story you can watch unfold from an open jeep at dawn.

Assam's grasslands look almost prehistoric at first light, mist lifting off the swamp as a rhino's armoured grey bulk emerges from the reeds to graze. The species was hunted to a few hundred animals last century; today Kaziranga alone holds over two thousand, grazing alongside wild water buffalo, swamp deer and, if you are lucky, a tiger crossing the track ahead of the jeep.

The park is split into ranges — Central, Western, Eastern and Burapahar — and each has a different character, from open floodplain to denser forest edge, so a two-day visit covering more than one range is worth the extra permit. Early starts matter enormously here: the grass is at its shortest and the animals most active in the hour after the gates open.

Kaziranga closes entirely during the monsoon floods, so plan a visit between November and April when the park is dry and accessible. Add an elephant-back safari for a different vantage into grass too tall to see over from a jeep, though book it the evening before — slots fill fast in peak season.

slots.sample: Budapest runs on hot water and low light, and a weekend here should too.

Start on the Buda side for the view: Fisherman's Bastion and the Matthias Church at golden hour, with the Danube and the lit-up Parliament building spread out below. Cross the Chain Bridge into Pest as evening falls, when the whole riverfront turns gold and every photograph looks like a postcard.

Spend a morning at the Szechenyi thermal baths, the grand yellow palace of a bathhouse where locals play chess waist-deep in steaming water regardless of the season. Book a slot early on a weekend — Szechenyi gets crowded by midday, and the outdoor pools are worth reaching before the queues do.

After dark, head to the ruin bars of the Jewish Quarter — Szimpla Kert is the famous one, built into a derelict building with mismatched furniture and a courtyard cinema, but the smaller bars on the same streets are worth a wander too. Order a fröccs, the local wine spritzer, and let the night run later than planned; Budapest's best hours often start after most cities have gone quiet.

slots.sample: A cog railway older than the resort it climbs from carries you to one of the great mountain views in the Alps without a single step of walking.

The train leaves from a small station just behind Zermatt's main street, a red cogwheel carriage that starts climbing almost immediately into larch forest. There is no engine pulling you — a toothed rack under the train grips a matching rail on the track bed, which is how it manages gradients no ordinary train could hold. It has run this way, largely unchanged in principle, since 1898.

The forest thins around Riffelalp and opens into rock and snow, and somewhere past Riffelberg the Matterhorn stops being a postcard and starts filling the window. Sit on the right-hand side going up for the best angle. At Gornergrat itself, 3,089 metres up, you step out onto a viewing terrace surrounded by thirty-eight named peaks over four thousand metres — the Matterhorn, Monte Rosa, the Gorner Glacier spilling down between them.

Go early. The first trains up catch the mountain lit gold before the crowds and before the afternoon cloud that often builds by midday arrives. There is a simple restaurant at the top if you want to linger over coffee with that view rather than rushing back down.

Zermatt itself is car-free, reached only by train from Täsch — so the Gornergrat is really the second act of a journey that starts the moment you leave your car behind. Bring layers regardless of season; the temperature drop between the village and the summit station is dramatic even in July.
Freya Lindqvist

slots.sample: In the forest around Harads, in Swedish Lapland, a cluster of architect-designed cabins hang among the pines, each one built to a completely different idea of what a treehouse could be.

No two cabins here look alike — one is a mirrored cube that all but disappears into the canopy, another resembles a giant bird's nest woven from branches, another a UFO suspended on cables. What they share is a bridge or rope-and-ladder approach up into the trees and, once inside, surprisingly serious comfort: underfloor heating, proper beds, and large windows angled to frame the forest rather than the ground below.

There is a communal sauna at ground level, usually wood-fired, and evenings tend to be spent there or simply sitting at a cabin window watching the light change — this far north, summer nights barely darken and winter ones are long enough for the aurora to appear directly overhead. Meals are typically taken together in a central lodge built from reclaimed timber.

Book well ahead, since each design has only one or two units and they fill fast, and come for a winter stay if you can manage the cold: watching the northern lights move across the forest canopy from inside a warm treehouse is the single best reason to make the trip.
Yuki Tanabe

slots.sample: Near Torres del Paine, a scatter of transparent geodesic domes lets you fall asleep under the same granite peaks you spent the day hiking toward.

The domes themselves are the draw: canvas-and-timber geodesic shells with a wide clear panel set into the roof, so from bed you can watch the Patagonian sky — usually startlingly clear and, in season, streaked with the southern aurora or the thick band of the Milky Way. Interiors are simple and warm rather than luxurious, built to survive the region's famous wind rather than to impress.

Because most domes have no private bathroom, guests share a central refugio building for showers, meals and the wood-fired stove that becomes the social hub after dark, where hikers compare notes on the day's routes toward the towers or the French Valley. The lodges typically arrange transfers and guided treks directly from the property, useful given how remote and weather-dependent this part of Chile can be.

Book shoulder season — spring or autumn — for thinner crowds and darker skies, and pack for real cold: the dome's canvas walls and glass ceiling look romantic but do little to hold heat once the Patagonian wind picks up at night.
Kwame Mensah

slots.sample: The world's longest railway turns a map into a lived experience, one time zone at a time.

You board in Moscow with a paper ticket, a compartment number, and roughly nine thousand kilometres ahead of you. The first day is birch forest and provincial stations, the platforms crowded with babushkas selling smoked fish and boiled potatoes through the carriage windows during the longer stops. Time stops mattering in the usual sense — you start living by the train's Moscow-time clock instead of the sun outside.

Compartment life has its own rhythm: glasses of tea in metal holders from the samovar at the end of the carriage, games of cards with whichever nationality you happen to be sharing a cabin with, long silent stretches watching taiga scroll past for hours without a single building. Pack more food than you think you need — the dining car is inconsistent, and the best meals come from platform vendors at Yekaterinburg and Irkutsk.

Break the journey at Lake Baikal — most travellers stop in Irkutsk and take a side trip to Listvyanka or Olkhon Island, where the world's deepest lake sits impossibly blue against the hills. It resets you for the final push through the Russian Far East to Vladivostok, where the railway meets the Pacific and the whole continent-crossing scale of the trip finally lands.

Book a second-class kupe compartment rather than the open-plan platzkart if you want a door that closes, and bring a Russian phrasebook — English thins out fast east of the Urals. The provodnitsa (carriage attendant) runs your world for a week; a friendly relationship with her matters more than any guidebook.
Mateo Duarte

slots.sample: A felucca, the lateen-sailed boat of the Nile, offers the slowest and finest way to drift past Aswan's islands and temples.
Sailing the Nile the old way

A felucca is the traditional wooden sailboat of the Nile, and a night aboard one near Aswan is the antidote to the cruise-ship version of Egypt. There is no engine and no schedule — the boatman reads the wind, you lie back on cushions, and the river slides by past palm-fringed islands and villages where children wave from the bank.
As the sun drops, the sails glow and the temperature finally eases. Dinner is simple, cooked on board, eaten by lamplight.
A night on the water
Sail up to Elephantine Island and the Nubian villages with their painted houses.
Bring a warm layer — desert nights are cold even when the days are furnace-hot.
Sleep on deck under a mosquito net and wake to mist rising off the river.

It is rustic, unhurried and gloriously low-tech. For a night or two, the felucca strips Egypt back to wind, water and a horizon of date palms — the way travellers have crossed this stretch of the Nile for centuries.
Omar Benali

slots.sample: A self-drive loop through Namibia trades the crowds of East Africa's safari circuits for some of the emptiest, most dramatic landscapes on the continent.

Start at Sossusvlei, where dunes among the tallest in the world rise in shades of apricot and deep rust against a bone-white pan. Set an alarm well before dawn and climb Dune 45 or Big Daddy in the cool dark — the light as the sun clears the ridge line turns the sand from grey to burning orange in a matter of minutes, and the heat afterwards makes clear why nobody climbs at midday. Deadvlei, a claypan of centuries-dead camel-thorn trees against that same orange sand, is a short walk further and just as striking.

Drive west to the coast at Swakopmund for a change of register entirely — a tidy German colonial town wrapped in cold Atlantic fog, where the desert meets the sea in dunes that tumble almost into the surf. It's a strange, welcome contrast after the heat inland, and a good place to service the car and restock before heading north.

Etosha National Park closes the loop with some of the most reliable wildlife viewing in Africa, largely because you do the work of a guide yourself: park at a floodlit waterhole near your camp after dark and simply wait. Elephant, rhino and lion all pass through on their own schedule, sometimes within touching distance of the fence, and the patience required is a fair trade for watching it unfold without another vehicle in sight. Namibia's distances are vast and fuel stops are few, so top up the tank whenever you see one rather than waiting until you need it.
Hana Novak

slots.sample: Tucked east of Madagascar and still officially part of France, Réunion packs an active volcano, three vertiginous cirques and a ring of black-sand coast into a single small island.

Piton de la Fournaise, one of the world's most active volcanoes, is also one of the more approachable — a marked trail crosses the Plaine des Sables, a lunar expanse of red and black volcanic rock, before climbing to the crater rim in around two to three hours each way. Check activity levels before you go; the volcano erupts fairly often, and access is closed without much notice when it does, which is honestly part of the appeal.

The island's three cirques — vast eroded calderas ringed by cliffs — are the real reason hikers make the trip, and Mafate is the most remarkable of the three: a village-dotted basin with no road access at all, reachable only on foot or by helicopter. Stay a night in a gîte in La Nouvelle or Marla, where dinner is typically a communal table of rougail sausage and rice, and the silence after the generators switch off is close to total.

Balance the interior with a few coastal days around St-Gilles or St-Leu, where black volcanic sand gives way to a genuine coral lagoon protected from the open ocean swell — one of the only safe swimming stretches on an island whose Atlantic-facing coast is otherwise rough and shark-flagged. Réunion runs on French time and euros despite being closer to Madagascar than to Europe, so pack accordingly and expect a long-haul flight connection through Paris for most non-regional visitors.
Priscila Rocha

slots.sample: Beyond the day-trip dunes of Merzouga, multi-day treks into the Sahara trade jeep tracks for camel trains and star-thick silence.

Most visitors see the Erg Chebbi dunes on a sunset camel ride and a night in a fixed camp, but a proper trek pushes further south past Merzouga into the erg's interior, where a small camel train carries water and supplies and the only sound for hours is sand shifting underfoot.

Days settle into a rhythm of walking in the cool morning, resting through the worst of the midday heat under a shared tarp, then climbing a high dune to watch the light turn the sand from gold to rose before making camp and eating tagine cooked over a buried fire.

Go between October and April to avoid the worst heat, trust your Berber guide's read of the dunes over any GPS — sand shifts and landmarks move — and pack layers for the cold that arrives fast after sunset, since desert nights drop sharply once the sand stops holding the day's heat.
Kwame Mensah

slots.sample: Thermals off Sarangkot ridge carry paragliders over Phewa Lake with the Annapurna range filling the horizon.

Pokhara is ranked among the world's best paragliding sites for a simple reason: launch from Sarangkot ridge at 1,600 metres and reliable thermals can keep a glider airborne for well over half an hour, circling above Phewa Lake with the snow line of the Annapurna and Machapuchare massif filling the entire northern horizon.

Tandem flights need no experience — a certified pilot handles launch, thermals and landing while you take in a view that combines a Himalayan skyline with a lakeside city few other flying sites can match, and vultures often share the same thermal, banking a wingspan away.

Fly in the clearer pre-monsoon months of autumn or spring for the best mountain visibility, book with a pilot registered under Nepal's paragliding association rather than the cheapest tout on the lakefront, and land assuming a slightly bumpy touchdown on the lakeside strip — it's part of the ride.
Hana Novak

slots.sample: Cables, ladders and rungs bolted into WWI battlefields let hikers climb Dolomite rock faces that would otherwise need ropes and a rack.

The via ferrata network across the Dolomites was largely built during the First World War to move troops through the mountains, and today those same iron cables, ladders and rungs let hikers with a harness and two lanyards climb terrain — the Tofana di Rozes, the Lagazuoi — that would otherwise require full rock-climbing kit.

Clipping and unclipping past each anchor point becomes second nature within an hour, but the exposure never quite does, especially on routes like the Ferrata Ivano Dibona where a ledge narrows to a boot's width above several hundred metres of air.

Start on a grade-1 route like the Ferrata delle Trincee before attempting anything harder, rent a proper via ferrata kit with a shock-absorbing lanyard rather than improvising, and check the weather obsessively — an afternoon thunderstorm on an exposed cable is the single biggest danger in these mountains.

slots.sample: A Eurail or Interrail pass can be genuinely cheap or a wasted purchase, and the difference comes down to how deliberately you plan around it.

Passes pay off on countries with long distances and pricey point-to-point fares — Germany, Switzerland, and Scandinavia reward a pass far more than Spain or Italy, where discounted advance tickets on high-speed lines often beat the pass on a per-journey basis. Before buying, price out your actual route both ways: add up what individual tickets would cost, then compare it to the pass tier that covers your travel days, and only buy if the pass wins by a meaningful margin.

Almost every high-speed and night train across Europe requires a separate seat reservation even with a valid pass, and those reservations cost extra and sell out — book them the moment reservations open on popular routes like Paris–Barcelona or any Nightjet sleeper. A flexi pass with a set number of travel days within a longer window suits an itinerary with rest days built in; a continuous pass suits people who intend to move almost daily.

Track your travel days like a budget, not an afterthought — a single day pass covers unlimited trains within that one calendar day, so it's worth building itineraries around days with two or three short hops rather than spreading them across separate days. Download the operator's app for real-time platform changes, since passes don't exempt you from needing a specific train and coach number on reservation-required services.
Freya Lindqvist

slots.sample: Points and miles can genuinely fund a chunk of your travel, but the beginner mistake is chasing every sign-up bonus instead of picking one ecosystem and learning it properly.

Pick a single major transferable-points programme to start — the kind that lets you move points to multiple airline and hotel partners rather than a card locked to one airline's own miles. Transferable points are more flexible when redemption values shift, and they let you shop around for whichever partner airline offers the best value for a specific route rather than being stuck with one airline's often-poor economy redemptions.

Redemption value is where beginners lose the most money: booking a domestic economy flight with points that could have funded a long-haul business seat is technically 'free' but a poor use of the currency. Learn roughly what your points are worth in cents per point for a few realistic redemptions before you book anything, and hold off spending them on the first flashy option that appears.

Only carry a card with an annual fee if you can quantify what you get back — a free checked bag, airport lounge access, or a points bonus that clearly outweighs the fee. Set a calendar reminder before any sign-up bonus's minimum spend deadline, and never carry a balance to chase points; the interest wipes out any value the points were worth many times over.
Kwame Mensah

slots.sample: Vietnam rewards the thrifty traveller: cheap sleeper trains, dollar bowls of pho and guesthouses that cost less than a city coffee back home.
The whole country on a shoestring

Vietnam is one of the great value destinations, and travelling it end to end — Hanoi in the north to the Mekong Delta in the south — can be done comfortably on a modest budget. Overnight trains and sleeper buses cover the long distances cheaply and save you a night's accommodation into the bargain.
Street food is the secret: a bowl of pho or a banh mi costs a couple of dollars and beats most restaurant meals hands down.
Stretching the budget
Take the Reunification Express in stages; soft-sleeper berths are cheap and comfortable.
Eat where the plastic stools are full of locals, not where the menu has photos.
Rent a motorbike for a day in places like Ha Giang or the Hai Van Pass.
Allow three or four weeks to do it justice without rushing. Travel slowly, eat on the street, take the night transport, and Vietnam gives you an extraordinary amount of country for very little money.
Inés Carvalho

Nothing prepares you for Gold Harbour — a beach on South Georgia so densely packed with king penguins that the shoreline itself seems to move.
The Galápagos is the rare place where wild animals simply ignore you, letting you sit an arm's length from a blue-footed booby without it so much as breaking stride.
Every October, polar bears converge on the shoreline near Churchill, Manitoba, to wait out the days until Hudson Bay freezes solid enough to hunt seals again.
A slow boat along Sabah's Kinabatangan River turns up more wild orangutans in an afternoon than most people see in a lifetime of nature documentaries.
Nothing in East Africa matches the noise and nerve of a wildebeest column throwing itself into the crocodile-thick Mara River at the height of the migration.
The Pantanal's flooded rivers hold the best odds on Earth of watching a wild jaguar hunt in daylight, from the low seat of a skiff.
The Okavango Delta is a rare inland river that never reaches the sea, and the quietest way to experience it is from a hand-poled mokoro sliding silently between the reeds.
Yala holds one of the highest densities of leopards anywhere on the planet, and unlike most big-cat destinations, here the odds of a sighting genuinely favour you.

The resplendent quetzal's iridescent tail and improbable colouring have drawn birders to Costa Rica's high cloud forest for decades, and the valley of San Gerardo de Dota remains the surest place to find one.

slots.sample: A car and eight days are all you need to trade island-hopping crowds for the Peloponnese's ancient theatres, Byzantine towns and empty beaches.

Nafplio makes the best base for the first few days — a handsome Venetian port town with two fortresses to climb and none of the cruise-ship pressure of Athens. From here, Epidaurus is a half-hour drive; the ancient theatre's acoustics are famous enough that guides still demonstrate them by dropping a coin on the stone floor of the orchestra, audible from the very top row.

Head south into the Mani peninsula, a wilder stretch of stone tower villages and cactus-lined roads that feels a world away from the postcard islands. Stop at Mystras on the way, a Byzantine hill city abandoned to the elements, its frescoed churches and crumbling palaces climbing a slope beneath the walls of a Frankish castle — go early, before the heat and the tour buses arrive.

Finish on the western coast at Voidokilia, a near-perfect horseshoe of sand backed by dunes and a ruined castle, or push further to the causeway beaches around Elafonisos if you have an extra day to spare. The roads through the interior are slow and mountainous, so budget more driving time than the map suggests, and keep a full tank — petrol stations thin out fast once you leave the main coastal routes.
Omar Benali

slots.sample: Skip the Algarve crowds and head inland, where whitewashed hill towns and terraced vineyards show a slower, older Portugal.

Évora is the natural place to start: a walled university town with a Roman temple standing incongruously in the main square and a bone chapel that draws more visitors than either. Rent a car here rather than on the coast — the Alentejo's appeal is in its emptiness, cork oak plains rolling to the horizon with barely another vehicle in sight, and public transport between the small towns is sparse at best.

Push on to Marvão, a fortified village perched so high on a granite ridge that on a clear day you can see into Spain. Stay a night if you can; the day-trippers leave by five and the narrow streets empty out into something close to silence, broken only by swifts wheeling around the castle walls at dusk.

From there it's a half-day's drive north to the Douro Valley, where terraced vineyards climb near-vertical slopes above the river in a landscape that looks engineered rather than grown. Base yourself in Pinhão and take one of the small wooden rabelo boats out onto the water in the late afternoon — the light on the terraces then is the reason painters have been coming here for two centuries, and most quintas along the river will pour you a glass of port to go with the view.
Freya Lindqvist
